declarations.description:
Carries a host's ARIA references down to the control inside it.

**The gap this closes, measured.** `<helix-button aria-describedby="tip">` puts
the description on the host, and the host is not what a reader is on: the
accessibility tree exposes the `<button>` in the shadow root, and the host
beside it is a generic with a description nobody hears. Read from Chrome's own
tree:

```
host           role=generic  name=""       desc="Helix description"
inner button   role=button   name="Helix"  desc=""
```

A plain `<button>` with the identical attribute reads `desc="Helix
description"`, so the reference itself is fine and only its destination is
wrong. This moves it.

**An IDREF cannot make that trip and an element reference can.** The ids are
written in the consumer's tree and the control is in a shadow root, so
`aria-describedby` copied onto the inner element resolves to nothing.
`ariaDescribedByElements` takes the elements themselves, and a reference is
valid into the same tree *or a shadow-including ancestor* of it: from inside
the shadow root looking out, the document is exactly that. Measured, the
assignment reads back with the node intact, where the inward direction, from a
light-DOM trigger to a node in a shadow root, reads back empty. This is the
one direction that works, which is why `Tooltip` needs `for` and this does
not.

**The attributes stay on the host.** Nothing is removed and nothing is added:
the consumer's markup is exactly what they wrote, which is the same reason
`hostAria` exists. What changes is only that the control now also holds the
reference, so a screen reader on the focused element hears it.

Watched with a `MutationObserver`, because a reference can arrive at any time:
a framework rendering a tooltip after this element upgrades, or a consumer
pointing `aria-describedby` at a different id, changes an attribute and
nothing schedules a Lit update.
declarations.name: AriaForwardController

`aria-describedby` naming a heading that has been removed is a stale
reference, and an empty array clears the property rather than leaving the
last good one in place.

declarations.description:
Which reading a pointer is nearest, for a chart that draws no markers.

**The anchor is a position and not an element, and that is the whole reason
this exists.** A bar and a donut slice are elements a tooltip could be hung
on; a line is one `<path>` for a whole series, because
`preserveAspectRatio="none"` turns a circle into an ellipse and there is no
vector-effect that answers for a shape, so `LineChart` deliberately draws no
per-reading marker. Anchoring per datum works for two charts of four and
cannot be extended to the third, so the resolution is arithmetic instead.

**It maps along one axis only.** The nearest reading to a pointer is decided
by x alone in a vertical chart, whatever y is doing, because a reader moving
across a chart is asking about a column of it rather than about a point. A
true nearest-point search would make a two-series chart answer differently
depending on which line the pointer drifted toward, which is a tooltip that
changes its mind while the reader holds still.

**Coarse pointers get nothing.** A touch has no hover, so a tooltip driven by
one appears where a finger already covers it and stays after the finger
lifts. The table underneath is the readable version and is what a phone
should be given, so this listens for `pointermove` and ignores anything whose
`pointerType` is not fine.
declarations.name: ChartPointerController

members.description: The reading under the pointer, or -1 when the pointer is elsewhere.

members.name: axis
members.description:
Which axis the readings are laid out along.

**An axis and not a boolean, because two of the four charts do not use x.**
A horizontal bar chart runs its categories *down* the box, so resolving
every reading from the pointer's x leaves a move from the first row to the
last never changing the answer: measured on four rows, all four reported
the third, which is the slot the middle of the box falls in. It looks like
a tooltip that will not follow and is a tooltip reading the wrong axis.

`none` is the ring. Its slices are real elements at every angle, so the
reading under the pointer is the one the pointer is over, and arithmetic on
either axis would answer with whichever slice shared a coordinate: at three
o'clock and at nine o'clock, x alone gives the same slice for opposite
sides. The slices call `set` and this only holds the answer.

members.description:
Tells the tooltip its anchor moved, which nothing else would.

The mark the tooltip is hung on is one element the chart walks from reading
to reading with an inline style, and Floating UI's `autoUpdate` watches
scrolling, resizing and layout shift. Moving an absolutely positioned
element by writing `inset` is none of the three, so the bubble is placed
once on open and then stays where the first reading was while the mark
travels out from under it.

Here rather than in the chart because the reading is this controller's, and
after the update rather than in `set` because the mark is still at the old
position until the render that follows.

The host also holds the row of labels, so measuring against it would map

chart started measuring down the box rather than across it, which is what
`axis` is for: on a horizontal bar chart the labels are beside the plot
rather than under it, and the host is wider than the drawing by exactly
their column.

declarations.name: supportsInvokers
declarations.description:
Whether the browser implements invoker commands.

Feature-detected on the prototype rather than on an instance, so it can be
answered before anything has rendered, and guarded for a server, which has no
`HTMLButtonElement` at all.

The `command` event, for a browser that does not send one.

Invoker commands are recent: Chrome 135, Firefox 137, Safari 18.4. Before
this, a button in an older browser set `commandForElement` on nothing, the
wiring silently did not happen, and the control did nothing at all when
clicked. No error, no warning, and every `command` in the library dead at
once, which is the worst way for a feature to be missing: the markup is
right, the component is right, and the button is simply inert.

So the button sends this instead where the platform will not. It carries the
two members `CommandController` reads and dispatches at the target, which is
where the platform dispatches too, so nothing downstream can tell the
difference.

**The built-in commands are not reproduced.** `show-modal`, `close` and
`toggle-popover` are defined against native elements and applied by the
browser itself, and writing our own would mean reimplementing part of the
platform against elements we do not own. Nothing in this library uses them:
a custom element only ever answers a `--` command, which is the platform's
marker for "the target decides", and the target is ours.
declarations.name: HelixFallbackCommandEvent

declarations.description:
Lets a control elsewhere on the page operate this one, declaratively.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
<helix-dialog id="confirm">…</helix-dialog>
```

**The platform's own invoker, not a convention of ours.** `commandfor` and
`command` are attributes the browser understands: it resolves the id, wires
the two together, and dispatches a `command` event at the target when the
trigger is activated. That is a real event with a real source, so it works
for a click, for Enter, for Space, and for anything else the platform decides
counts as activation later.

A `data-` recipe of our own would mean a delegated document listener a
consumer cannot see, an id lookup and activation semantics we would write
ourselves, and a convention that is ours to document and theirs to learn.

**Only custom commands reach a custom element.** The built-in ones
(`show-modal`, `close`, `toggle-popover`) are defined against native elements
and the browser applies them itself; pointed at a custom element they do
nothing. So the names here start with `--`, which is the platform's marker
for "the target decides what this means", and the target deciding is exactly
what this is.

Unrecognized commands are left alone rather than swallowed, so a host that
answers `--show` does not quietly absorb a `--print` meant for something
else.
declarations.name: CommandController

declarations.description:
Puts text on the clipboard and holds a confirmation for a moment.

A controller rather than a component, because copying is a behavior and not a
shape. Color's chip is a swatch that copies, and a copy button is a button
that copies, and those two have nothing in common to look at: what they share
is the write, the confirmation that follows it, the timer that ends it and the
event that announces it. Written twice, the second one would get the failure
case wrong.

**There are two routes and both are tried**, because the modern one is gated
in more places than it looks and a control that does nothing is
indistinguishable from a broken one. See `write` above.

**Where neither route is allowed, the failure is silence.** The confirmation
does not appear, which is the honest report: a message about a clipboard is
worse than a chip that did not flash, and there is nothing a reader could do
about a permission policy anyway.

**The event is announced after the write, not before it.** It is not
cancelable for the same reason: by the time anything could be said, the text
is already on the clipboard, and an event that cannot prevent what it
describes should not pretend otherwise.

The timer is cleared when the host leaves the document, or a component removed
mid-confirmation asks a detached element to re-render.
declarations.name: CopyController

declarations.description:
Pushes a group's `disabled` onto its members, on every update, unasked.

**The cascade itself is `inheritDisabled`, and this is what makes it
automatic.** Called by hand it runs only when whichever method holds the call
runs, so a group whose items changed by some other path leaves them holding
the last answer, and a group that forgets the call gets no cascade at all
with nothing to say so: the property exists, the attribute reflects, and the
members simply ignore it. That is invisible in review and shows up only when
someone disables a set.

It adds no API. A group already has `disabled`, from `HelixFormElement` or
from the consumer; nothing here introduces a property or a method for anyone
to call. By this repo's own rule that makes it a controller and not a mixin:
it reacts to a lifecycle and nothing else.

So a group states its members once, at construction, and never thinks about
it again:

    new DisabledCascadeController(this, { items: () => this.items })

**Runs after every render, and on every `slotchange`.** The second half is
not an extra: a member arriving in the light DOM changes no property, so Lit
schedules nothing, and a render-only cascade leaves a member slotted into an
already-disabled group enabled. Measured before it was added, on a radio
group holding two disabled members with a third inserted: `110`, and the
third was live in a set nobody could use.

The listener is on the render root rather than on the host, because
`slotchange` bubbles but is not composed: it reaches the shadow root that
owns the slot and stops there. On the host it would never fire at all.

After render rather than before, because the items are read from the DOM and
a newly slotted member is not there until the render that assigns it.

Idempotent, so running on every update costs a comparison per member and
nothing else: `inheritDisabled` writes only where the answer changed and
remembers what each member said for itself, which is what lets a group be
re-enabled without freeing a member that was disabled on its own.
declarations.name: DisabledCascadeController

declarations.description:
Closes an overlay on Escape or on a pointer press outside it.

Both, because they are different intentions with the same meaning: Escape is
the keyboard's way out and clicking away is the pointer's, and an overlay
that honors only one is one half its readers cannot dismiss.

The outside press is watched on `pointerdown` rather than `click`, so a press
that starts outside and drags across the overlay still counts as leaving
rather than as interacting.

A press inside a frame is the third case, and it needs its own signal. The
frame swallows the event, so the document that owns the overlay never sees a
`pointerdown` at all, and where the frame is cross-origin there is nothing to
listen to inside it either. What is observable is that the window lost focus
and a frame on this page gained it, which is exactly a press the document
cannot see. Leaving the browser altogether blurs the window too, so what took
focus is the part that distinguishes them.

declarations.description:
One page of a nested set showing at a time, with a way back.

A drill-down replaces the panel rather than opening a second one beside it.
That is the right shape wherever there is no room for two: on a phone there
is no second column, and on a touch screen there is no hover to open one
with. What a reader gets instead is one panel, a title saying where they are,
and a way back.

**None of this is about menus.** A settings panel, a filter stack or a
navigation tree gets the same behavior without being a menu that is
pretending.

**The tree is the state.** A row's page is its own children, assigned to a
slot, so the controller holds one reference, the row currently drilled into,
and derives everything else from the DOM. The alternative, an id per page and
a map beside it, is a second copy of the structure that a consumer can put
out of step with the first.

**A stack, not a pointer.** `back()` returns to the page above rather than to
the root, because a reader three levels down pressed one control and expects
one level. The stack is rebuilt from the DOM by walking up from the current
row, so it cannot disagree with the tree: a page removed while it was showing
takes its ancestors with it, and `atRoot` becomes true rather than the
controller holding a reference to something detached.

Nothing here decides what a row *is*, what it renders, or what happens when
one is chosen. It answers where the reader is and what is on this page.
declarations.name: DrilldownController

members.name: here
members.description:
The row whose page is showing, once the tree has been asked about it.

**A held reference can outlive the row it names, and the walk alone does
not catch it.** Removing the row a reader is *on* works: its
`parentElement` is null and the walk stops. Removing one of its
*ancestors* does not, because the subtree comes away intact, so the child
still has a parent and the parent still has a parent. Measured on a
three-level menu with the middle page removed: `depth` answered 2, `rows`
listed a page nobody could see, and `back()` walked to a second detached
row before reaching the top.

That is the disagreement with the tree the walk exists to prevent, so the
question is asked here, once, and every reader below goes through it.

declarations.description:
Places one element against another, and keeps it there.

Positioning is `@floating-ui/dom` rather than arithmetic written here. Two
things in particular are why. A `position: fixed` element inside an ancestor
carrying `transform`, `filter`, `will-change`, or `contain` is positioned
against that ancestor and not the viewport, so viewport coordinates land it
somewhere else entirely. And an overlay has to clear its nearest *clipping*
ancestor, not just the window, or it is placed correctly inside a scrolling
panel and clipped out of sight by it. Both are ordinary here, and both are a
long tail of browser behavior rather than a formula.

`autoUpdate` keeps the position through scrolling on any ancestor, resizes of
either element, and layout shifts.

The side the element actually landed on is written back as `data-placement`,
so a styled tier can animate from it rather than from the side that was
asked for.

**The custom properties are declared here because this is what writes them.**
Each carries a measurement taken against the viewport that no stylesheet can
take for itself, and `core` ships no CSS, so there is no reader inside this
package and none of them is private. the `hooks` rule pairs a documented
hook with a rule that reads one, in both directions.

question is whether anybody still wants it.

declarations.description:
Measures the marked child and writes the geometry onto a traveling mark.

Serves `Navigation`, `Tabs`, `Toggle.Group` and `Outline`. The two things
hand-written copies of this get wrong:

**The inline axis is signed.** In a right-to-left document the distance is
measured from the surface's right edge and applied as a negative translation,
because the mark travels from the inline start and the inline start is on the
right. Measuring from the physical left and applying an unsigned offset from
the inline-start edge sends the mark the wrong way in RTL.

**The border has to come off both axes.** `getBoundingClientRect` gives the
border box and the containing block is the padding box, so a surface with a
border of its own puts the mark one border-width out. `clientLeft` and
`clientTop` are the border widths, already resolved, which is why they are
used here rather than parsing `borderLeftWidth`.

**Nothing is written until there is something to measure.** A zero-width box
is a component whose children have not upgraded yet, and writing zeroes would
park the mark at the origin and leave it there. The `data-placed` attribute is
what a stylesheet waits for, so a mark fades in where it belongs rather than
sliding from the corner on first paint.

The four custom properties are the contract. What a component does with them
is its own business, which is how one controller serves a bar under a tab, a
pill filling it, and a rule down the side of a contents page.

**Declared here because this is what writes them.** `core` ships no CSS, so
every reader is outside this package and none of these is private.
the `hooks` rule pairs a documented hook with a rule that reads one, in both
directions.

declarations.description:
Moves through a set of items with the arrow keys, and chooses as it goes.

**Moving and choosing are one act here, not two.** That is the radio group
pattern and it is the difference from a listbox: moving focus without
choosing leaves a keyboard reader sitting on an item they have not selected,
with nothing on screen saying which of the two is true. A pointer user
chooses by arriving, so a keyboard user does too.

**Both axes, always.** A vertical set still answers left and right, and a
horizontal one still answers up and down. Binding only the axis the items
happen to be laid out on means a reader who guesses wrong gets nothing, and
`orientation` is presentation: the same set of choices reads the same way
whichever direction it runs.

Disabled items are skipped rather than stopped at, so a set with a gap in it
still moves in one press.

A set that starts from focus rather than from the selection, or that moves
without choosing, says so through `origin` and `selects`. Neither is a reason
to keep a hand-written copy, and neither exempts a set from both axes.
declarations.name: KeyboardNavigationController

declarations.description:
A surface that floats against something, in the top layer, until dismissed.

Bundles the three things that always travel together: the popover API, a
`FloatingController` and a `DismissController`.

**The top layer is the whole point.** A floating panel has to escape every
clipping ancestor between it and the page, and `position: fixed` does not do
that: it is clipped by `overflow` on any ancestor and re-anchored entirely by
an ancestor carrying `transform`, `filter` or `contain`. The popover API
lifts the element out of the tree's paint order for real, and it is the only
thing that does.

`manual` rather than `auto`, because the host owns dismissal. `auto`
popovers light-dismiss themselves and close each other, which is close to
what is wanted and not the same: a select that closed itself before its own
change event landed, or a submenu that closed its parent, are both things the
platform would do here and neither is right.

**The order matters on the way up.** `showPopover` first, then position:
measuring an element that is still `display: none` gives zeroes, so a surface
positioned before it is shown lands at the origin and slides into place on
the next frame. On the way down it is the reverse, and stopping the observer
before hiding avoids a final measurement of an element on its way out.

What this does not own is *when*. Opening is the host's, because a menu opens
on click, a tooltip on hover and a select on either, and none of that is
about surfaces.
declarations.name: PopoverController

declarations.description:
Resolves the element a chart reads from, and follows it.

Every chart that takes a `for` wants exactly this, and wants it to behave
identically, so it is a controller rather than a paragraph in each of them.

A controller and not a pure function, by the test the rules set: it reacts to
the host's lifecycle. It has to start watching when the host connects, stop
when it leaves, and re-resolve when `for` changes.

**What it refuses is as much the point as what it accepts.** A `<table>` or
anything built from grid roles, including this library's own `helix-table`,
whose roles live in `ElementInternals` and therefore write no attribute at
all. Anything else resolves to null, so a `for` pointed at a paragraph draws
nothing rather than something arbitrary.

The element is watched for `childList` and `characterData` alike, because
renaming a series edits a text node in place rather than replacing a cell,
and nothing in a page has reason to know a chart is reading it.
declarations.name: SourceController

Points the watcher at whatever `for` names now.

Called on connect and by the host when `for` changes. Safe to call when

declarations.description:
Reads a design token as the sRGB triple a shader or a 2D canvas can take, and
tells the host when the palette underneath it moves.

**Two hops, and both are load-bearing.** A custom property's own value is the
unevaluated function text, so `getComputedStyle` on a probe is the only way
to see what it resolves to. And what it resolves to is not `rgb()`: the
palette derives from an `oklch()` seed, and Chrome answers `lab(100 0 0)` for
white. Parsing that with a regular expression for numbers reads the three
channels as 100, 0 and 0, which divided by 255 is a dark red.

A screenshot cannot catch that: a warm cast on a saturated gradient is also
what chroma subsampling produces, so the picture agrees with the bug.

The conversion is therefore the browser's own: fill a pixel and read it back.
That holds for `lab()`, `oklch()`, `color-mix()` and whatever a token is
written in next, which is the property worth having in a design system whose
palette is derived rather than listed.

**A controller and not a mixin**, by this repository's own line: it adds no
property or method a consumer sets. It reacts to lifecycle, holding a probe
that has to be created after the host connects and removed when it leaves,
and it watches for the color mode changing so the host can repaint.

**Client only, and that is the contract rather than a limitation.** There is
no computed style on a server and no canvas to convert with, so `read`
answers the fallback there. Every caller is drawing into a canvas, which does
not exist on a server either.
declarations.name: TokenColorController

declarations.description:
Works out which slice of a long set is worth rendering.

**A controller and not an element, which is the whole reason it is here.**
Table, Listbox, Combobox and Tree each need windowing *inside* themselves,
and an element would make each of them nest one in its own shadow root: a
listbox whose options are inside a `<helix-virtual-list>` is a listbox whose
options are no longer its children, so its own keyboard, its own selection
and its own ARIA all have a stranger in the middle of them.

**A windowed set still reports its true length, and each row its true
position.** This is the part virtualization usually gets wrong and the reason
the arithmetic lives somewhere shared. A reader on row 4,000 of 10,000 must
hear "4,000 of 10,000", so `aria-setsize` is the count and `aria-posinset` is
the real index, never the position within the rendered slice. The window is a
rendering decision and the set is a fact, and a component that lets the first
overwrite the second has told a screen reader the list is twelve long.

**The spacers are what make the scrollbar honest.** Rendering twelve rows in
a box that should scroll for ten thousand gives a thumb the size of the
track, so the room the absent rows would have taken is left as padding before
and after. A reader dragging that thumb is dragging against the real length.

**What it does not do, and the reason is narrower than it first looks.** True
virtualization means never creating the rows that are not on screen, and that
needs the set as *data*. Two channels are shut: a consumer's items arrive as
light-DOM children, which exist by the time this could decide not to create
them, and an `items` property cannot survive React hydration, which skips
every property it would have to apply imperatively (see `bindReactHandler`,
and the note in the rules that objects and functions have that bug and are
not fixed).

**A third channel is open.** Data as *text*
in the markup, a `<script type="application/json">` child or an attribute, is
neither a property nor a node per row: React's hydration bug cannot touch text
it renders as a child, a server emits it, and the node count is one. The
charts already read data out of the document this way, `for="<id>"` at a real
`<table>`, so the pattern is in the library rather than being invented for
this.

So the thing actually blocked is the *row template*. Turning an item into
markup wants either a render function, which is a function property and dies
on the same bug, or a `<template>` with named holes, which survives because it
is markup and which no component here asks anyone to write. That is a decision
about what this library is willing to look like, not a platform limit, and it
is open at #71.

So what this buys is the expensive half rather than all of it: the rows
outside the window are not laid out and not painted, which is where the time
goes in a long list, and the node count stays. That is worth having and it is
not worth calling something it is not. An element that windows children it
was handed is not a virtual list, whatever it is named.

**One estimate, not per-row measurement.** Measuring every row to place it is
how a virtual list ends up reading the layout it is trying to avoid, and it
is what makes them jump: a row taller than its estimate shifts everything
after it at the moment it renders. A fixed estimate is a straight line
between scroll offset and index, which never disagrees with itself. Rows of
genuinely different heights are a different component and a harder one.
declarations.name: VirtualizeController

Says once that the box cannot be measured, and why.

A warning rather than a throw, because the list still works: it holds a

the window well, and that is the consumer's stylesheet to fix, not
something this can decide on their behalf.

Once per controller, because a warning per frame is one people filter out
and this one has to be believed the day it is right.

declarations.description: Records the events a set of tags dispatch. Called by generated code.

declarations.name: eventsForTag
declarations.description: The events a tag dispatches, or `undefined` if nothing registered it.

Fired when an element is about to open.

Cancelable: `preventDefault()` refuses the change, and the element stays
closed. Paired with `helix-before-close` rather than being one event carrying a
boolean, so a listener that only cares about one direction says so by which
event it listens for.

Neither bubbles nor composed. A dialog inside a drawer inside a popover is
three overlays, and an inner one opening must not read as the outer one
opening.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeOpenEvent

declarations.description: Fired when an element is about to close. See `HelixBeforeOpenEvent`.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeCloseEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when the reader asks for the next thing in a set.

Paired with `helix-previous` rather than being one event carrying a
direction, which is the reason `helix-before-open` gives for its own pair: a
listener that only cares about one direction says so by which event it
listens for. The detail carries the direction anyway, so a consumer who does
want one handler can have one.

Bubbles and is composed, because the thing that answers this is usually not
the thing that asked. A video has no notion of a set: it plays one resource,
and what comes next is a playlist's business or the consumer's, so the event
has to reach a wrapper.

Not cancelable. There is no default action to refuse: the component that
fires this does nothing on its own, and an event whose `preventDefault` means
nothing is an event that lies about what it offers.
declarations.name: HelixNextEvent

declarations.description: Fired when the reader asks for the previous one. See `HelixNextEvent`.
declarations.name: HelixPreviousEvent

declarations.description:
A stop asking the tour to move.

Composed and bubbling, because a stop is slotted into the root and the root
has to hear it across that boundary.

**A class rather than a hand-rolled `CustomEvent`.** A dispatch is matched as
`new HelixSomethingEvent(`, so a raw `CustomEvent` is not held to being
declared and nothing carries it into the manifest: consumers can hear it and
cannot find it.
declarations.name: HelixTourAskEvent

declarations.description:
The eyedropper opening, and closing again.

Two events rather than one carrying a flag, because what a consumer does with
them is not symmetrical: the surface holding the picker has to get out of the
way for the sample and come back afterwards, and those are two moments with
different work in each.

**A class rather than a bare `Event`.** The check that holds an event to being
declared reads `new Event(` as well as `new HelixSomethingEvent(`, so a
hand-rolled one is public API a consumer can hear and cannot find.

No detail, because there is nothing to say beyond that it happened.
declarations.name: HelixSampleStartEvent

declarations.description: The eyedropper closing, whether or not a color was taken.
declarations.name: HelixSampleEndEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when an element asks to be taken away.

A request rather than a notification: the element does not remove itself,
because the consumer owns the markup it is in and removing the node under
them would put their state and the document out of step. Cancelable, so
`preventDefault()` is a refusal.

One verb for both shapes. A tag leaving a list and an announcement closing
itself are the same act from the element's side.
declarations.name: HelixDismissEvent

declarations.description:
A set is about to make a different child current, and can be refused.

**Not a generic `helix-change`.** `Tabs` moving to another tab, `Tree` marking
another row and `Steps` advancing are not a value changing, they are a set
choosing, and the platform's word for a committed value would say the wrong
thing. `active` names which child is current, so `activate` is the verb, and
unlike `change` the platform has no claim on it.

**This fires before the state moves.** Inside a handler `currentTarget.active`
still holds the previous value, and `detail.value` is a proposal another
listener may refuse, so a consumer who only wants to know which child is
current listens for `helix-activate` instead. `helix-select` is not that
notification either: it fires when an item is *chosen*, not when `active` is
assigned.

The shape is the one `MixinControllerOpen` already has, a cancelable request
and a plain notification after the state has moved.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeActivateEvent

declarations.description:
A set has made a different child current.

The notification half of `helix-before-activate`, dispatched after the state
has moved, so `currentTarget.active` is the new value and the detail is a fact
rather than a proposal.

**Not cancelable**, for the reason every notification here is not: the
decision was taken by the event before it, and a second refusable event for
one transition is two answers to one question.

**Prefixed, and it has to be.** `activate` unprefixed is not in any
`*EventMap` in the DOM library, checked rather than assumed, but the prefix is
what stops an event dispatched inside a shadow root and retargeted to the host
being mistaken for something the host's own contents sent.
declarations.name: HelixActivateEvent

declarations.description: A message is about to be pinned or unpinned, and can be refused.
declarations.name: HelixBeforePinEvent

declarations.description: A divider is about to move, and can be refused.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeResizeEvent

declarations.description:
The divider between a sandbox's panes is about to move, and can be refused.

Its own verb rather than a `helix-before-resize` carrying which divider moved:
a sandbox has two, and they were told apart by a field on a detail every other
request in this file also carries.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeSplitEvent

declarations.description:
A sandbox's panel is about to change height, and can be refused.

The sibling of `helix-before-split`, and named for the divider rather than for
the axis because a reader binding one of the two is choosing which divider they
care about. `value` is pixels here and a percentage there, which is what each
property already publishes.
declarations.name: HelixBeforePanelResizeEvent

declarations.description: A pane is about to collapse or reopen, and can be refused.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeCollapseEvent

declarations.description: Source is about to be edited, and can be refused.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeEditEvent

declarations.description:
A value is about to change, and the change can be refused.

**The request half of every value control.** It announces the value being
*proposed*, before anything moves, so a listener calling `preventDefault()`
refuses it and the control stays where it was. That is how a consumer takes
one decision without declaring a mode, which is what 294 settled: the element
always owns and applies its state, and refusing is the way to take it over.

**The notification is native and separate.** Once this has gone out and the
value has moved, the control announces it again under the platform's own
name, `input` while a reader is editing and `change` when they are done, so
`onChange` in React and `onchange=` in HTML both reach it and
`currentTarget.value` is correct by the time a handler reads it. This event
carries the detail because at the moment it fires the value is not on the
element yet.

**`announcesInput` picks which native notification fires, not which name this
carries.** Granularity is the platform's own distinction, `input` against
`change`; the request is always this one event.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeChangeEvent

declarations.description:
A checked state is about to change, and the change can be refused.

**Its own event rather than a `helix-before-change` carrying a boolean.**
Through the value event the state arrives as `String(checked)`, so a consumer
receives the string `"false"`, which is truthy, and a test asserting the value
passes on that bug. A control whose state is a boolean wants an event with a
typed boolean in it.

The notification is native, as it is for a value: the control relays `change`
from the inner input and announces `input` beside it, so `onChange` reads
`currentTarget.checked` and gets a boolean from the platform.

It also ends a collision: Checkbox Group listened for its boxes' change and
dispatched its own under the same name from the same host, so it needed
`stopImmediatePropagation` to keep a consumer from receiving one box's boolean
alongside the whole set. Two names, two facts.
declarations.name: HelixBeforeToggleEvent

declarations.description:
The reader asked for something the list does not hold.

Cancelable, and announced before anything is applied, because the options are
the consumer's own light DOM and no component here writes into it. What the
control can do is say what was asked for and take the value; putting an
option in the list, or a row in a database, is the consumer's, and a consumer
who validates first refuses this and adds nothing.

The detail carries the text as typed, not a slug of it. Trimming or lowering
it here would be this element deciding what a name means, and a consumer who
wants an identifier can make one from what they were given.
declarations.name: HelixCreateEvent

declarations.description:
Something was copied to the clipboard.

Not cancelable, and deliberately: it is announced after the write, because a
clipboard write is a permission the platform may refuse and there is nothing
useful to report until it has either happened or not.
declarations.name: HelixCopyEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when something being previewed writes to the console.

Carries text rather than the logged values. The preview is a separate
document, so what arrives has crossed `postMessage` and been through
structured clone: a DOM node or a function does not survive that, and half a
value is worse than a string of it.
declarations.name: HelixConsoleEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when something reports how much room its content actually needs.

**A measurement crossing a boundary the measurer is on the far side of.** A
sandboxed preview is its own document: nothing outside it can read the height
of what it drew, because the frame is opaque and a box sized from the outside
only ever reports the box. So the document measures itself and says so, and
this is what it says it with.

A number rather than a box, because the width is the container's to decide and
only the block size follows the content. A consumer that wants to act on it
clamps it: what arrives is what was drawn, which for an empty example is
nearly nothing and for a long one is more than a page.
declarations.name: HelixResizeEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a header crosses the threshold between resting at the top of the
page and floating over it.

**The threshold lives in a custom state, and is announced rather than
reflected.** A `data-scrolled` on the host is an attribute nobody rendered: a
server sends the element without it and the element adds it on upgrade, so a
framework hydrating the page finds markup that no longer matches what it sent.
A custom state is deliberately not in the DOM and therefore not something a
hydration pass can disagree with.

That closes the observability an attribute would accidentally provide. A
`MutationObserver` can watch an attribute and there is no equivalent for
`ElementInternals.states`, so a component holding a boolean nothing can read
is a component with a private opinion its consumers demonstrably need: the
bar's own backdrop is drawn by the page around it, and the page has to know
when to light it.

Not cancelable. It reports where the page is rather than asking permission to
be there, and refusing it would leave the state and the announcement
disagreeing.

The hysteresis stays inside the header, which is the point of announcing at
all: a consumer listening to `scroll` itself would be a second opinion on
when the page counts as scrolled, and the two would part company at the eight
pixels of travel this waits for.
declarations.name: HelixScrolledEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when the cursor moves in a text editor.

Not cancelable, unlike everything else here. The others announce something
about to happen and a listener can refuse it; this one reports where the
caret already is, and there is nothing left to refuse.

It fires on every keystroke and every arrow press, which is why the status
bar reads it from the DOM rather than through a framework's state: routing a
caret position through React would re-render the workbench on every cursor
move.
declarations.name: HelixCaretEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a component moves the view it is showing, rather than its value.

A calendar paging to another month is not choosing a date, and the two have
to be separable: a consumer driving the view needs to hear that it moved
without being told the answer changed. `helix-change` belongs to the value,
and giving it both jobs would make either one unusable on its own.
declarations.name: HelixNavigateEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a control that fills up has filled.

The moment a code entry exists for: a six-character field is worth submitting
the instant the sixth character lands, and a consumer watching `helix-change`
has to know the length and compare it on every keystroke to find that moment
themselves.

Separate from `helix-change` rather than a flag on it, because they are
answered by different code: one keeps a value in step and the other decides
whether to send a form. A listener that only cares about the second says so by
which event it listens for.

`complete` is free as a verb. React's synthetic system claims `change`,
`input`, `submit`, `reset`, `copy`, `paste`, `scroll`, `drag`, `focus` and
`blur`, measured, and this is none of them.

Not cancelable. It reports that something already happened, which is the same
reason `helix-caret` is not: there is nothing left to refuse once the last
character is in the box.
declarations.name: HelixCompleteEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when the reader offers something they wrote.

**Cancelable, and the composer clears only when nobody refused.** Sending is a
round trip: a composer that empties itself and then hears the request failed
has thrown away the only copy of what the reader typed, and a reader who has
just written three paragraphs is exactly who cannot afford that. Refusing
leaves the text where it is.

Not `helix-create`, which is the combobox's event for a value a list does not
hold, and not `helix-change`, because nothing about a value changed: the
reader finished something and handed it over.
declarations.name: HelixSendEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when something a user comes back to is marked read, or unread.

**Read state is reported rather than owned.** Marking a notification read is
usually a round trip, and a component that flips the state itself and then
hears the request failed has already told the reader something untrue. So this
is cancelable, and refusing it leaves the item alone; a component left
uncontrolled applies it once nobody has refused, which is the same contract
every other axis in the library uses.

Bubbles and is composed, so a feed hears its own items: one handler on the
list serves every notification in it, which is what a consumer syncing to a
server actually wants.
declarations.name: HelixReadEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when the reader asks for a different order.

Cancelable, and refusing it leaves the order alone, which is what makes a
server-side sort expressible: the consumer refuses the local reorder, fetches,
and hands back a new set. This is the element reporting that a heading was
clicked, before it acts on it.

Not `helix-change`: nothing about the data changed, only the order it is read
in, and a consumer listening for changes to a value should not hear a sort.
That is the same distinction `helix-filter` is drawn on.
declarations.name: HelixSortEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a component narrows what it is showing.

Filtering hides rather than removes, so nothing about the value changes and
`helix-change` would be a lie. What a consumer wants to know is that the list
in front of the reader is no longer the whole list.
declarations.name: HelixFilterEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a shortcut's chord is pressed.

Cancelable, and the key event is only consumed where this is not refused: a
consumer that decides the moment is wrong, a dialog is over the control or
the reader is mid-composition, calls `preventDefault()` and the keystroke
goes on to whatever would have had it.
declarations.name: HelixShortcutEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when the reader selects an item in a set.

Bubbles and is composed, because this is how a set coordinates: a tree, a
tab list and a toggle group all learn which of their children was chosen by
hearing it arrive.
declarations.name: HelixSelectEvent
helixEventNames
declarations.description:
Every name this library dispatches.

Exported so a runtime check can ask whether a name is one of ours without
keeping a second list of them. `HelixElement` uses it to tell a consumer that
the handler prop they wrote is attached to nothing.

Owns only what is universal: normalizing `box-sizing` inside the shadow root,
so component CSS can rely on border-box on both sides of the boundary.

There is deliberately no `emit(name, detail)` helper. A dispatch through a
generic helper cannot be named by the manifest analyzer, which recorded the
parameter identifier and produced a phantom event on every element that
inherited it. Components dispatch concrete event classes from `events.ts`,
which the analyzer and TypeScript can both see.
declarations.name: HelixElement

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

**The public tag may not be the composed one, in either tier.** Using it
costs three things: the name means two different things depending on what a
consumer imported, the headless tier composes an element it does not ship,
and the composition cannot be tested there at all, because there is no
`helix-select` on that tier to test it against.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument; `checked`, `open`,
`invalid` and `has-label` are recorded the same way, each of them a state a
`default-*` attribute resolves before React reaches the node.

**Deferring the definitions is not a fix and could not be.** Importing them
from an effect so the upgrades fall the other side of hydration works only
while hydration is one pass: anything that splits it, a streamed segment or
a suspended boundary, puts an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot
be the guarantee when the fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` is written around.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was

members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing else does, so without this a control inside a disabled fieldset
stays fully typeable and announces itself as enabled.

The submission half is already the platform's: measured, the fieldset's
controls are absent from the form's entry list and the host matches
`:disabled`, so the value never goes anywhere. What is missing without this
is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.description:

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

control with a `default-value` would serve empty and fill itself at

component, because what an empty value means is the component's business: a
text field submits its emptiness, since `""` is an answer and the field was
on the form, while a group with nothing chosen submits nothing at all.

*when it is on* rather than what it holds, so it is configuration rather than
state, and the state it does have is `checked`, which is

declarations.description:
Grafts a label, help text, and a validation message onto a control.

**Over `HelixElement` rather than `HelixFormElement`, because not every
control that wants a label is form-associated.** A checkbox group is the
case: each box in it submits itself already, so the group deliberately
reports no value of its own, and every form-related member of
`ElementInternals` throws `NotSupportedError` on an element that is not
form-associated. Measured, and the ARIA members are fine on the same
element, which is why the naming and describing work there and only the
validity has to ask first.

Every form control wants the same three things around it and wants them in a
different arrangement: a label above an input, beside a checkbox, and over a
group. So this owns the properties, the parts, and the wiring, and each
control places the nodes where its own geometry needs them. Same part names
either way, so one stylesheet in the styled tier dresses all of them.

**Not a wrapping `Field` component, and that is not a style preference.** A
wrapper cannot name what it wraps. Its label would live in its own shadow
root and the control in another, and measured in Chrome 148: an
`aria-labelledby` IDREF cannot see across, and
`control.ariaLabelledByElements = [labelInTheWrapper]` reads back as zero
elements, the reference dropped. The same assignment with a label in the
control's own tree is kept. That pattern works in React libraries because
they have no shadow boundary; bringing it here brings the ergonomics and none
of the conditions that made it work.

**A control whose label is its content renders its own.** A checkbox is named
by the words beside it, inside the `<label>` that forwards the press, so it
uses its default slot and nesting `renderLabel`'s `<label>` in there would be
invalid markup. `label` is that slot's fallback either way.

Worth knowing, because it costs a label and gives no warning: **a
whitespace-only text node is assigned to the default slot and defeats its
fallback.** Measured in Chrome 148, and a newline between the tags is enough,
so `<helix-checkbox label="Accept">` closed on the next line renders no label
at all. A named slot does not have this problem, because `slot="label"` is an
attribute and a text node has none. It is the platform's behavior rather
than ours, and the same is already true of every slot fallback here.

**The ids are fixed rather than generated.** IDREFs resolve within the tree
that holds them, so two controls on a page each carrying `helix-hint` in
their own shadow root do not collide. That also removes the usual hydration
hazard, since there is no generated value for a server and a client to
disagree about.

**A group has to say it differently.** A control's `<input>` and its hint
are both in the shadow root, so a plain `aria-describedby` resolves. A
group's host is in the light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot
reach and `element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference. Only
`internals.ariaDescribedByElements` keeps it, which is what `describeHost`
uses. Measured the same way, and the failure is silent either way: the
description simply never reaches the accessibility tree.

**The label, the hint and the feedback are documented on each component that
applies this, rather than here.** Declaring them once on this mixin is the
obvious fix and does not work: the analyzer reads `@csspart` off a custom
element class, so a class-level tag here reaches the manifest as nothing at
all, on this JSDoc and on the inner class alike. Measured both ways, and the
inner-class version is the dangerous one, since it satisfies the rule while
every API page stays exactly as wrong as before. Members are different and
do inherit, which is what the note about the inner class in the area rules
is about.
